title: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Limited range of forms in small organisms”. Scope: bacteria and micrococci

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-16: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Identification accuracy across controlled domain shifts is a direct test, and extensive public labeled bacterial phenotype and image data exist. The historical word 'seldom' needs a threshold, but comparative performance can robustly resolve the central claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Train and validate species classifiers using cell-shape features from bacteria imaged across life stages, growth conditions, and preparation methods, and compare performance with physiological or genomic identifiers. The claim is supported if morphology generalizes poorly across conditions while nonmorphological identity remains stable.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern high-dimensional morphology may outperform the simple visual criteria Thompson meant.

Repository species labels and imaging protocols may be imbalanced.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data existence: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: BacDive can test the identification half directly: many species share a shape class, so form seldom names the species. It does not systematically record plasticity across life stage, medium and preparation, which is the mechanism the claim gives for that failure. The open data therefore resolve a proxy, morphological non-specificity, and leave the plasticity statement only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Ask how often cell shape class uniquely identifies a bacterial species, and how much shape of the same strain changes with growth phase, medium and preparation. Low identifiability together with large within-strain shape change would support the claim; shape that stably diagnoses species across conditions would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most strains carry one curated shape, not a series across life stages and preparations.

Physiological specificity is a much larger character set than the shape field.

Shared rod or coccus shapes show low identifiability even when each species is morphologically stable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.6
data existence: 0.75
analysis feasibility: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.5
